What marketing works best in the slow season?

8 min read

The slow season is the most valuable marketing window of the year, because you finally have time to do the work that compounds. Reactivate past customers, publish seasonal content, build reviews and profile assets, and run targeted offers for off-season work. The contractors who market when it’s quiet are the ones who skip the next dry spell entirely.

“Leads come in bursts after a storm, then it goes quiet for weeks.” Every roofer has said some version of it, and every trade lives some version of it — the feast-or-famine cycle that makes cash flow a white-knuckle ride. Here’s the reframe that changes everything: the slow season isn’t a weather problem. It’s a marketing problem. The dry spells happen because nothing was planted during the last busy stretch. The fix is to treat the quiet months as your most important marketing window of the year — because for once, you actually have time to do the work that pays off later.

1. Reactivate your past customers (the highest-ROI move there is)

The single best lead source contractors name, over and over, isn’t a platform or an ad — it’s past customers and referrals. They already trust you. They’ve already paid you. And most contractors completely forget about them the moment the job ends.

The slow season is when you reconnect:

  • Send a simple email or postcard to everyone you’ve worked for. A maintenance reminder, a seasonal tip, a “we have openings this month” note. Low effort, high return.
  • Offer off-season maintenance or tune-ups. The exact services people forget about are perfect for filling slow weeks — and they keep your name in front of customers before their next big job.
  • Ask for referrals directly. A happy past customer will often hand you a neighbor if you simply remind them you’re available.

This is the marketing with the best return and the lowest cost, full stop. It’s why “build an email list of past customers” shows up in every honest breakdown of lead sources for contractors.

2. Build the assets you’re too busy to build in season

During peak months you can’t breathe, let alone build content. The slow season is your workshop. This is when you create the things that bring in leads automatically once business picks back up:

  • Write seasonal service pages and blog posts. Answer the questions homeowners Google before they call — “how do I know if I need a new roof,” “why is my furnace short-cycling.” Publish in the slow season so they rank by the time demand returns. Our guide to service pages that rank walks through the formula. (For seasonal/repeat-demand trades, blogging earns its keep precisely because it answers what people search before they buy.)
  • Deepen your Google Business Profile. Add photos from the season’s jobs, fill in every field, post updates. A richer profile ranks better — see our optimization guide.
  • Clean up your website. Fix the slow pages, update the gallery, sharpen the copy. The repairs you never have time for in July.

3. Stack reviews for the rebound

Reviews are roughly 20% of local ranking and the trust signal that converts browsers into calls. The slow season is the perfect time to circle back to recent customers you never got around to asking and request that review. A surge of fresh five-star reviews heading into your busy season lifts your ranking right when search volume climbs. Our review guide makes it a system instead of a scramble.

4. Run targeted offers for off-season work

Some work is genuinely seasonal, but plenty isn’t — it’s just not top of mind. A focused slow-season promotion can pull that demand forward:

  • Off-season pricing or scheduling perks — “book your spring project now and lock in winter rates.”
  • Inspections and tune-ups that catch problems early and tee up bigger jobs later.
  • A small, focused ad budget on the high-intent searches that still happen year-round. Paid clicks are often cheaper when competitors pull back.

What NOT to do: go dark

The instinct when money’s tight is to slash marketing entirely. It’s the worst possible move, and it’s exactly why the cycle repeats. Marketing has a lag — what you do in the slow season produces leads in the busy one. Cut it now and you guarantee another famine later. Notably, 72% of home-services businesses plan to increase marketing budgets in 2026, and the smart ones aren’t spending evenly — they’re investing in the quiet months precisely because that’s when the groundwork gets laid and the competition goes quiet.

The whole point: stop riding the rollercoaster

Feast-or-famine isn’t inevitable — it’s the signature of reactive marketing. Contractors who only hustle when the phone goes quiet stay trapped in the cycle. The ones who market through the slow season — reactivating customers, building content, stacking reviews, running smart offers — smooth the curve and walk into their busy season with a pipeline already full. The work you do when it’s quiet is exactly what makes it stop being quiet.

Frequently asked questions

What's the best marketing to do in the slow season?

Reactivating past customers, by a wide margin. They already trust you and have paid you, yet most contractors forget them the moment a job ends. A simple email or postcard with a maintenance reminder or seasonal offer is the lowest-cost, highest-return move there is, which is why past customers and referrals top every honest list of lead sources.

Should I cut my marketing budget when business is slow?

No — it's the single worst move and the reason the feast-or-famine cycle repeats. Marketing has a lag, so what you do in the slow season produces leads in the busy one. Cut it now and you guarantee another dry spell later. Notably, 72% of home-services businesses plan to increase budgets in 2026, and the smart ones invest in the quiet months.

Is blogging worth it for a contractor?

For seasonal and repeat-demand trades, yes. Blog posts answer the questions homeowners Google before they call — like how to tell if they need a new roof — and the slow season is the ideal time to write them so they rank by the time demand returns. Done right, that content brings in leads automatically once business picks back up.

How do I avoid the feast-or-famine cycle?

Treat the slow season as your most important marketing window instead of going dark. Reactivate past customers, publish seasonal content, stack fresh reviews, and run targeted off-season offers. Because marketing produces leads on a lag, the groundwork you lay when it's quiet is exactly what fills your pipeline before the next busy season starts.
